newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia raps NATO, Solana denies anti-Moscow policy.
newsitem.headline: Russia raps NATO, Solana denies anti-Moscow policy.

text.p: The Kremlin accused NATO and its Secretary-General Javier Solana of pursuing a covert anti-Moscow policy on Wednesday, prompting swift denials by the alliance and raising tensions over its eastward expansion plans.

President Boris Yeltsin's press secretary, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, said Solana had "undeclared, behind-the-scenes" aims in making a tour of four former Soviet republics with which Moscow is trying to strengthen ties.

"The West as a whole, and the leadership of NATO in particular, is opposed to any form of political or military integration between the newly independent states -- the republics of the former USSR, especially when they are initiated by Moscow," Yastrzhembsky told Interfax news agency.
"Having called such a line an anti-Moscow one, the press secretary noted that it was perceived by Russia 'no doubt without sympathy, but with concern'," Interfax said.
Officials at the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's headquarters in Brussels responded quickly to the denunciation of Solana's trip to Moldova, Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan.

"NATO does not regard at all the relationship between these countries and NATO and the relationship between these countries and Russia as mutually exclusive," one source told Reuters. "One does not exclude the other," the source added.

Later Solana himself defended his right to visit members of NATO's Partnership for Peace programme, which is designed to forge closer ties between former Cold War foes. Russia is also a member of the programme.
"I don't see why a visit to these countries must be interpreted as a secret agenda of NATO," a clearly agitated Solana told reporters in the Armenian capital Yerevan.
Wednesday's exchange pointed to new strains in ties between NATO and Russia over the alliance's plans to take in former Warsaw Pact member states from eastern and central Europe.
Russian officials say NATO's plans threaten its security, create new divisions in Europe and undermine Yeltsin's grip on power, already weakened by ill health.

Moscow's campaign had reached a new peak on Tuesday when one official said Moscow should be ready to use nuclear weapons if subjected to an attack with conventional arms, although the Kremlin later distanced itself from those comments.

But Yastrzhembsky's remarks turned the volume even higher and were amplified by a new warnings from Defence Minister Igor Rodionov in an interview with a German magazine that Moscow would take "appropriate measures" if NATO expansion goes ahead.

The verbal offensive appears designed to win Moscow as many concessions as possible over expansion. It also reflects deep frustration at a lack of progress in talks on forging a "special relationship" with NATO to soften the blow of enlargement.

Russia wants the right to joint decision-making on issues which concern its "vital interests" and says progress at talks on revising a treaty setting levels on conventional weapons in Europe will show how ready the West is to seek a deal.
Time is running out for reaching a deal before a NATO summit in July at which the alliance is expected to issue membership invitations to Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary.

The attack on Solana suggested Moscow may want to sideline him and pin its hopes of progress on a proposed summit of leaders from Germany, Russia, the United States, Britain and France, although Washington has not backed the planned meeting.

Yeltsin's foreign policy adviser, Dmitry Ryurikov, criticised Solana's tour on Tuesday and Yuri Baturin, secretary of Russia's advisory Defence Council, openly defied calls by Solana for Moscow to remove troops from Moldova's Dnestr region.

In the Georgian capital Tbilisi on Wednesday, Solana said NATO enlargement was inevitable but Moscow had misconeptions about the alliance's plans and was wrong to think it would be left out of a new European security system.
"So far Russia has shown some interest. But there still remain many misconceptions and stereotypes in Russia's thinking about NATO," Solana told the Georgian parliament.
He reiterated the alliance's promises not to position nuclear weapons on the territory of new member states.
